headline: High: Continue’s filesystem/MCP tool use can collide with Argo Workflows’ API-driven orchestration, creating default-path prompt, data, and action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read workspace files and use MCP/tool calls, so attacker-controlled content in files or MCP outputs could influence its instructions. Argo Workflows exposes REST/GRPC APIs and handles artifacts/parameters, but no direct shared channel is documented. The pairwise pathway is plausible via files or API-fed content, so I rate it medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Continue is configured to ingest workspace files containing untrusted text, THEN prompt injection is possible.
IF an MCP server returns attacker-controlled content that Continue treats as instructions, THEN hijacking is possible.
mitigations: Restrict Continue to trusted folders only.
Disable or whitelist MCP servers.
Separate Argo artifact paths from editor workspace files.
Add a review step before acting on file-derived instructions.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for file and MCP content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and editor buffers and can send context to a user-chosen model provider or MCP server; Argo Workflows handles artifacts and parameters and has allowlisted egress. If Argo outputs sensitive artifacts into the same workspace, Continue may surface them to external services. The shared-file path is documented, so medium fits.
conditions: IF Argo writes sensitive artifacts or parameters into a workspace readable by Continue, THEN leakage can occur.
IF Continue is pointed at a remote model provider or MCP server, THEN workspace contents may leave the host.
mitigations: Keep sensitive Argo artifacts outside the IDE workspace.
Use local-only model providers for Continue.
Limit Continue’s file access to a narrow project subtree.
Rotate any exposed API keys or secrets immediately.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP/redaction before model submission.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue has write_filesystem, execute_shell, spawn_subprocesses, and broad network egress; Argo Workflows can call REST/GRPC APIs and emit artifacts/parameters. Even though Argo itself is not writable locally, the pair can concurrently mutate shared files or remote workflow state without coordination, and Continue’s filesystem sharing via host state makes conflicts likely. Uncertainty about exact shared targets pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same workspace files, THEN write conflicts can occur.
IF Continue uses shell or subprocess actions against files that Argo also updates, THEN race conditions can corrupt state.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Disable Continue write actions on shared paths.
Use read-only mounts for Argo outputs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can act on code and workspace content, while Argo can move artifacts and parameters through workflows. If Continue consumes Argo-produced outputs as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into edits or workflow actions. Argo does not verify Continue’s reasoning, and Continue’s tool use via MCP is user-approved but still operationally downstream, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF Continue treats Argo-generated artifacts or parameters as authoritative, THEN downstream errors can propagate.
IF a workflow output is copied into Continue without verification, THEN incorrect edits or actions can follow.
mitigations: Require human review of workflow outputs before reuse.
Add schema validation for artifacts and parameters.
Mark generated files clearly as untrusted.
Disable auto-apply for Continue suggestions.
requires-engineering: add provenance checks between workflow outputs and IDE actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Argo Workflows is open-source and only documented here as handling artifacts and parameters; Continue is an IDE extension touching source code and editor buffers with model-provider keys. No explicit residency or certification mismatch is documented, so only a low compliance risk is supportable. I do not cite both agents because this is a policy-mismatch assessment, not a shared-channel pathway.
conditions: IF sensitive code or parameters are subject to a stricter retention policy than the chosen model provider, THEN compliance gaps can arise.
IF Argo artifacts include regulated data and Continue sends them to a non-compliant provider, THEN policy violations occur.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Continue prompts.
Use a compliant/local model provider.
Document retention settings for both tools.
Review data-class handling before enabling the pair.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across systems.
